briefOverview: Peter heals a man lame from birth at the temple, then explains the miracle as the work of the risen Jesus and calls Israel to repentance. The speech frames Jesus as the fulfillment of the prophets and promises future restoration for those who turn back to God.
summary: At the afternoon hour of prayer, Peter and John encounter a man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate. Peter, having no money, commands him in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth to walk, and the man is immediately healed, leaping and praising God, which draws a crowd to Solomon’s Portico. Peter denies personal credit and attributes the healing to Jesus, whom the people handed over and denied before Pilate but whom God raised from the dead. He acknowledges their ignorance yet insists that God fulfilled what the prophets foretold about the Messiah’s suffering. Peter urges repentance and conversion so that sins may be blotted out and “times of refreshing” may come from the Lord, with Jesus remaining in heaven until the “restoration of all things.” He cites Moses’ promise of a coming prophet like him and the Abrahamic covenant, asserting that these days fulfill the prophetic hope and that God sent Jesus first to bless Israel by turning people from their iniquities.
externalContext: The ninth hour (about 3 p.m.) was a customary time of afternoon prayer at the Jerusalem temple, when crowds gathered and almsgiving was common. Public spaces like Solomon’s Portico on the temple’s east side were customary settings for teaching and debate. Early followers of Jesus in Jerusalem continued to attend the temple while proclaiming Jesus as Israel’s Messiah. In first-century Judea, the Roman prefect (such as Pilate) held ultimate authority over capital cases, though local leaders could influence outcomes, framing Peter’s mention of Pilate’s intent to release Jesus.
externalReferences: Peter’s identification of God as “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” echoes the divine self-identification in Exodus 3:6. His claim that Moses foretold a prophet “like me” directly cites Deuteronomy 18:15–19 and applies it to Jesus. The blessing to “all the families of the earth” recalls the promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 and 22:18. The healed man’s leaping evokes Isaiah 35:6, where the messianic restoration includes the lame leaping, and Peter’s reference to Jesus’ suffering fulfilled by the prophets aligns with Isaiah 53:3–5 and Jesus’ own teaching in Luke 24:25–27; the mention of Pilate reflects the Passion accounts (e.g., Luke 23:20–25).
practicalQuestions: When I lack material resources, how might I still serve others faithfully and boldly in Jesus’ name?
How do I handle public attention—do I redirect it toward God rather than myself?
Where might I need to repent so that “refreshing” and renewed fellowship with God can take root in my life?
How does this passage shape my view of Scripture’s unity, especially regarding promises fulfilled in Jesus?
In what ways can my community embody healing and restoration consistent with the gospel’s witness?
uncertainAreas: The exact identification of the “Beautiful” Gate is debated; the scope and timing of the “times of refreshing/restoration” are also open to eschatological interpretation, and the degree to which “ignorance” mitigates guilt is not fully specified in the text.
